From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia


First crewed Moon landing (1969)

"First Moon landing" and "The Moon landing" redirect here. For other crewed or uncrewed
Moon landings, see [Moon landing](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").

This article is about the 1969 crewed lunar mission. For other uses, see [Apollo 11 (disambiguation)](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").

**Apollo 11** (July 16–24, 1969) was the American [spaceflight](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") that first landed [humans](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") on the [Moon](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), and the fifth [crewed mission](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") of [NASA](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")'s [Apollo program](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"). The mission was crewed by Commander [Neil Armstrong](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), Command Module Pilot [Michael Collins](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), and Lunar Module Pilot [Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), all of whom were on their second and final spaceflight.

Launched atop a [Saturn V](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") rocket from [Kennedy Space Center](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") in [Florida](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") on July 16 at 13:32 [UTC](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), the Apollo spacecraft consisted of three parts: the [command module](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (CM), which housed the three astronauts and was the only part to return to Earth; the [service module](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (SM), which provided propulsion, electrical power, oxygen, and water to the command module; and the [Lunar Module](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (LM), which had two stages—a descent stage with a large engine and fuel tanks for landing on the Moon, and a lighter ascent stage containing a cabin for two astronauts and a small engine to return them to [lunar orbit](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"). After a three-day transit, Armstrong and Aldrin descended to the surface aboard the LM *[Eagle](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")*, landing in the Sea of Tranquility ([Mare Tranquillitatis](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")) on July 20 at 20:17 UTC while Collins remained in lunar orbit aboard the CM *[Columbia](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")*. Armstrong became the first human to walk on the
Moon approximately six hours after landing, followed by Aldrin nineteen minutes later.
Together they spent around two and a half hours walking on the surface, planting
an [American flag](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), speaking with President [Richard Nixon](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") who was in the [White House](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), deploying scientific instruments, and collecting
21.5 kg (47.5 lb) of lunar material. After more than 21 hours on the surface,
they rejoined Collins in lunar orbit, and the crew returned safely to [Earth](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") on July 24, splashing down in the [Pacific Ocean](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").

Apollo 11 was the culmination of the [Space Race](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), a geopolitical competition between the United States and the [Soviet Union](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") rooted in [Cold War](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") rivalry. It fulfilled a national goal set by President [John F. Kennedy](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") in May 1961, who had [challenged](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") the United States to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before the end of the decade. The program overcame a severe setback with the fatal [Apollo 1](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") launchpad fire in January 1967 and drew on technologies developed through the preceding [Mercury](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") and [Gemini](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") programs. The Soviet Union, despite early leads in spaceflight, was unable to match the Saturn V rocket, and its uncrewed lunar probe [Luna 15](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") crashed on the Moon on July 21, while Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin were still on the lunar surface.

Armstrong's moonwalk was broadcast live to an estimated 600 million viewers, roughly
one-fifth of the world's population, making it among the most-watched [television](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") events in history. Stepping onto the lunar surface, Armstrong declared: "[That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")." [Lunar samples](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") returned by the mission led to the identification of three previously unrecognized minerals, and scientific instruments deployed on the surface continued returning data for years afterwards. The crew were honoured with [ticker-tape parades](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), a world goodwill tour, and the [Presidential Medal of Freedom](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"). The command module
*Columbia* is preserved at the [National Air and Space Museum](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") in [Washington, D.C.](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), while the descent stage of
*Eagle* remains on the lunar surface.


## Background

In the late 1950s and early 1960s, the United States was engaged in the [Cold War](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), a geopolitical rivalry with the [Soviet Union](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").[[14]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched *[Sputnik 1](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")*, the first [artificial satellite](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), surprising the world and fueling fears about Soviet technological and military capabilities. Its success demonstrated that the USSR could potentially deliver [nuclear weapons](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") over [intercontinental distances](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), challenging American claims of military, economic, and technological
superiority.[[15]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

This incident sparked the [Sputnik crisis](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") and ignited the [Space Race](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), as both superpowers sought to demonstrate superiority in
spaceflight.[[16]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
President [Dwight D. Eisenhower](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") responded to the challenge posed by Sputnik by creating the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (NASA), and initiating [Project Mercury](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"),[[17]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
which aimed to place a man into [Earth orbit](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").[[18]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The Soviets took the lead on April 12, 1961, when [cosmonaut](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") [Yuri Gagarin](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") became the first person in space and the first to orbit the
Earth.[[19]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Nearly a month later, on May 5, 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space;
his 15-minute flight was suborbital, not a full orbit.[[20]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

Because the Soviet Union had [launch vehicles](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") with higher lift capacity, President John F. Kennedy, Eisenhower's successor, chose a challenge that exceeded the capabilities of the existing generation of rockets, so that both countries would be starting from an equal position. A crewed mission to the Moon would serve this
purpose.[[21]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

On May 25, 1961, Kennedy addressed the [United States Congress](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") on "Urgent National Needs" and declared:
"}},"i":0}}]}">.mw-parser-output .templatequote{overflow:hidden;margin:1em
0;padding:0 32px}.mw-parser-output
.templatequotecite{line-height:1.5em;text-align:left;margin-top:0}@media(min-width:500px){.mw-parser-output
.templatequotecite{padding-left:1.6em}}
> I believe that this nation should commit itself to achieving the goal, before this
decade [1960s] is out, of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the
Earth. No single space project in this period will be more impressive to mankind,
or more important for the long-range exploration of space; and none will be so difficult
or expensive to accomplish. We propose to accelerate the development of the appropriate
lunar space craft. We propose to develop alternate liquid and solid fuel boosters,
much larger than any now being developed, until certain which is superior. We propose
additional funds for other engine development and for unmanned explorations—explorations
which are particularly important for one purpose which this nation will never overlook:
the survival of the man who first makes this daring flight. But in a very real sense,
it will not be one man going to the Moon—if we make this judgment affirmatively,
it will be an entire nation. For all of us must work to put him there.


— Kennedy's speech to Congress[[22]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

On September 12, 1962, Kennedy [delivered another speech](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") before a crowd of about 40,000 people in the [Rice University football stadium](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") in [Houston](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"),
Texas.[[23]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[24]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
A widely quoted refrain from the middle portion of the speech reads as follows:
"}},"i":0}}]}">
> There is no strife, no prejudice, no national conflict in outer space as yet. Its
hazards are hostile to us all. Its conquest deserves the best of all mankind, and
its opportunity for peaceful cooperation may never come again. But why, some say,
the Moon? Why choose this as our goal? And they may well ask, why climb the highest
mountain? Why, 35 years ago, [fly the Atlantic](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")? Why does [Rice play Texas](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")?
> We choose to go to the Moon! We choose to go to the Moon ... We choose to
go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy,
but because they are hard; because that goal will serve to organize and measure the
best of our energies and skills, because that challenge is one that we are willing
to accept, one we are unwilling to postpone, and one we intend to win, and the others,
too.[[25]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
[![application/atom+xml](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:CentralAutoLogin/start?useformat=desktop&type=script&usesul3=1 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
President [John F. Kennedy](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") [speaking at Rice University](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") on September 12, 1962
In spite of that, the proposed program faced widespread opposition and was dubbed
a "[moondoggle](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")" by [Norbert Wiener](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), a mathematician at the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").[[26]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[27]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The effort to land a man on the Moon already had a name: [Project Apollo](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").[[28]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
When Kennedy met with [Nikita Khrushchev](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), the [Premier of the Soviet Union](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") in June 1961, he proposed making the Moon landing a joint project, but Khrushchev declined the
offer.[[29]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Kennedy again proposed a joint expedition to the Moon in a speech to the [United Nations General Assembly](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") on September 20,
1963.[[30]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The idea of a joint Moon mission was ultimately abandoned after Kennedy's death.[[31]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

An early and crucial decision was choosing [lunar orbit rendezvous](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") over both [direct ascent](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") and [Earth orbit rendezvous](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia"). A [space rendezvous](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") is an [orbital maneuver](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") in which two spacecraft navigate through space and meet up. In July 1962, NASA head [James Webb](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") announced that lunar orbit rendezvous would be
used[[32]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 -
Wikipedia")[[33]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
and that the [Apollo spacecraft](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") would have three major parts: a command module (CM) with a cabin for the three astronauts, and the only part that returned to Earth; a service module (SM), which supported the command module with propulsion, electrical power, oxygen, and water; and a lunar module (LM) that had two stages—a descent stage for landing on the Moon, and an ascent stage to place the astronauts back into lunar
orbit.[[34]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
This design meant the spacecraft could be launched by a single [Saturn V](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") rocket that was then under
development.[[35]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")

Technologies and techniques required for Apollo were developed by [Project Gemini](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 -
Wikipedia").[[36]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
The Apollo project was enabled by NASA's adoption of new advances in [semiconductor device](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia"), including [metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistors](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") (MOSFETs) in the [Interplanetary Monitoring Platform](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
(IMP)[[37]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 -
Wikipedia")[[38]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
and [silicon](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") [integrated circuit](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") (IC) chips in the [Apollo Guidance Computer](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
(AGC).[[39]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")

Project Apollo was abruptly halted by the [Apollo 1](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") fire on January 27, 1967, in which astronauts [Gus Grissom](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia"), [Ed White](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia"), and [Roger B. Chaffee](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") died, and the subsequent
investigation.[[40]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
In October 1968, [Apollo 7](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") evaluated the command module in Earth
orbit,[[41]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
and in December [Apollo 8](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") tested it in lunar
orbit.[[42]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
In March 1969, [Apollo 9](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "client-js vector-feature-language-in-header-enabled vector-feature-language-in-main-menu-disabled vector-feature-language-in-main-page-header-disabled vector-feature-page-tools-pinned-disabled vector-feature-toc-pinned-clientpref-1 vector-feature-main-menu-pinned-disabled vector-feature-limited-width-clientpref-1 vector-feature-limited-width-content-enabled vector-feature-custom-font-size-clientpref-1 vector-feature-appearance-pinned-clientpref-1 skin-theme-clientpref-day vector-sticky-header-enabled vector-toc-available skin-thumbsize-clientpref-standard") put the lunar module through its paces in Earth
orbit,[[43]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles")
and in May [Apollo 10](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles") conducted a "dress rehearsal" in lunar orbit. By July 1969, all was in readiness for Apollo 11 to take the final step onto the
Moon.[[44]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

The Soviet Union appeared to be winning the Space Race, but its early lead was overtaken
by the US [Gemini program](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") and Soviet failure to develop the [N1 launcher](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), which would have been comparable to the Saturn
V.[[45]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Seeing these failures, the Soviets then attempted to beat the US to return lunar
material to the Earth by means of [uncrewed probes](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"). On July 13, three days before Apollo 11's launch, the Soviet Union launched [Luna 15](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), which reached lunar orbit before Apollo 11. During descent, a malfunction caused Luna 15 to crash in [Mare Crisium](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") about two hours before Armstrong and Aldrin took off from the Moon's surface to return to earth. The [Nuffield Radio Astronomy Laboratories](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") radio telescope in England recorded transmissions from Luna 15 during its descent, and these were released in July 2009 for the 40th anniversary of Apollo
11.[[46]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

### Prime crew

|                      |
||--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------|
| -                    | -                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Commander            | [Neil Armstrong](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")<br>Second and last spaceflight          |
| -                    |
| Command Module Pilot | [Michael Collins](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")<br>Second and last spaceflight         |
| -                    |
| Lunar Module Pilot   | [Edwin "Buzz" Aldrin Jr.](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")<br>Second and last spaceflight |
| -                    |

The initial crew assignment of Commander [Neil Armstrong](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), Command Module Pilot (CMP) [Jim Lovell](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), and Lunar Module Pilot (LMP) [Buzz Aldrin](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") on the backup crew for
Apollo 9 was officially announced on November 20, 1967.[[47]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Lovell and Aldrin had previously flown together as the crew of [Gemini 12](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"). Due to design and manufacturing delays in the LM,
Apollo 8 and Apollo 9 swapped prime and backup crews, and Armstrong's
crew became the backup for Apollo 8. Based on the normal crew rotation scheme,
Armstrong was then expected to command Apollo 11.[[48]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

There would be one change. [Michael Collins](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), the CMP on the
Apollo 8 crew, began experiencing trouble with his legs. Doctors diagnosed
a bony growth between his fifth and sixth vertebrae, requiring surgery.[[49]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Lovell took his place on the Apollo 8 crew, and when Collins recovered he joined
Armstrong's crew as CMP. In the meantime, [Fred Haise](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") filled in as backup LMP, and Aldrin as backup CMP for Apollo
8.[[50]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Apollo 11 was the second American mission where all the crew members had prior spaceflight
experience,[[51]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
the first being Apollo 10.[[52]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The next was [STS-26](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") in
1988.[[51]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

[Deke Slayton](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") gave Armstrong the option to replace Aldrin with Lovell, since some thought Aldrin was difficult to work with. Armstrong had no issues working with Aldrin but thought it over for a day before declining. He thought Lovell deserved to command his own mission (eventually [Apollo 13](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")).[[53]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

The Apollo 11 prime crew had none of the close cheerful camaraderie characterized
by that of [Apollo 12](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"). Instead, they forged an amiable working relationship. Armstrong in particular was notoriously aloof, but Collins, who considered himself a loner, confessed to rebuffing Aldrin's attempts to create a more personal
relationship.[[54]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Aldrin and Collins described the crew as "amiable strangers".[[55]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Armstrong did not agree with the assessment, and said "all the crews I was on worked
very well together."[[55]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")


### Backup crew

|                      |
||----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------|
| -                    | -                                                                                                                                |
| Commander            | [Jim Lovell](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")     |
| -                    |
| Command Module Pilot | [William Anders](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") |
| -                    |
| Lunar Module Pilot   | [Fred Haise](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")     |
| -                    |

The backup crew consisted of Lovell as Commander, [William Anders](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") as CMP, and Haise as LMP. Anders had flown with Lovell on
Apollo 8.[[51]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
In early 1969, Anders accepted a job with the [National Aeronautics and Space Council](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") effective August 1969, and announced he would retire as an astronaut at that time. [Ken Mattingly](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") was moved from the support crew into parallel training with Anders as backup CMP in case Apollo 11 was delayed past its intended July launch date, at which point Anders would be
unavailable.[[56]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

Under the normal Apollo crew rotation, Lovell, Mattingly, and Haise would have been
assigned to [Apollo 14](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"). However, because [Alan Shepard](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") had only recently returned to flight status and needed additional training, NASA reassigned his crew to Apollo 14 and moved Lovell's crew up to fly [Apollo 13](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
instead.{{Cite web |date=January 30, 2019 |title=50 years ago, NASA names Apollo
11 crew |url=https://www.nasa.gov/feature/50-years-ago-nasa-names-apollo-11-crew
|access-date=February 24, 2023 |publisher=NASA}} Backup crews, according to the rotation,
were assigned as the prime crew three missions after their assignment of
backups."}},"i":0}}]}">[[a]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Shortly before launch, Mattingly was replaced by [Jack Swigert](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") due to concerns over possible measles
exposure.[[56]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")


### Support crew

During Projects Mercury and Gemini, each mission had a prime and a backup crew. For
Apollo, NASA added a third group, the support crew. Their job was to maintain the
flight plan, checklists, and mission rules, and to keep the prime and backup crews
updated on any changes. They also developed procedures—especially for emergencies,
so that by the time the prime and backup crews entered the simulators, they could
focus on practicing and mastering them.[[58]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The support crew for Apollo 11 was Mattingly, [Ronald Evans](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), and [Bill Pogue](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").[[59]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")


### Capsule communicators
[![application/atom+xml](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:CentralAutoLogin/start?useformat=desktop&type=script&usesul3=1 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
CAPCOM [Charles Duke](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (left), with backup crewmembers Lovell and Haise listening in during Apollo 11's descent
The [capsule communicator](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (CAPCOM) was an astronaut stationed at the [Mission Control Center](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") in [Houston](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), Texas, and was typically the only person permitted to communicate directly with the flight
crew.[[60]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
This practice ensured that messages came from someone best able to understand the
situation in the spacecraft and to relay guidance from [flight controllers](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") as clearly as possible. For Apollo 11, the CAPCOMs were backup and support crew members Anders, Evans, Haise, Lovell, and Mattingly, along with [Charles Duke](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), [Owen Garriott](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), [Don L. Lind](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), [Bruce McCandless II](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), and [Harrison Schmitt](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").[[59]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

## Preparations


### Insignia
[![application/atom+xml](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:CentralAutoLogin/start?useformat=desktop&type=script&usesul3=1 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
The Apollo 11 insignia. The eagle is carrying an olive branch to represent a peaceful
mission
The Apollo 11 [mission emblem](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") was designed by Collins, who wanted a symbol for "peaceful lunar landing by the United States". At Lovell's suggestion, he chose the [bald eagle](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia"), the [national bird](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") of the United States, as the symbol. Tom Wilson, a simulator instructor, suggested an [olive branch](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") in its beak to represent their peaceful mission. Collins added a lunar background with the Earth in the distance. The sunlight in the image was coming from the wrong direction; the shadow should have been in the lower part of the Earth instead of the
left.[[68]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")

Aldrin, Armstrong and Collins decided the Eagle and the Moon would be in their natural
colors, and decided on a blue and gold border. Armstrong was concerned that "eleven"
would not be understood by non-English speakers, so they went with "Apollo 11",[[68]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles")
and they decided not to put their names on the patch, so it would "be representative
of *everyone* who had worked toward a lunar landing".[[69]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

An illustrator at the [Manned Spacecraft Center](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (MSC) did the artwork, which was then sent off to NASA officials for
approval.[[68]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The design was rejected. [Bob Gilruth](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), the director of the MSC felt the talons of the eagle looked "too
warlike".[[70]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
After some discussion, the olive branch was moved to the talons.[[70]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
When the [Eisenhower dollar coin](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") was released in 1971, the patch design provided the eagle for its reverse
side.[[71]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The design was also used for the smaller [Susan B. Anthony dollar](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") unveiled in
1979.[[72]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")


### Call signs
[![application/atom+xml](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=startup&only=scripts&raw=1&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The original cockpit of the command module (CM) with three seats, photographed from
above. It is located in the [National Air and Space Museum](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"). The very high resolution image was produced in 2007 by the [Smithsonian Institution](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").
After the crew of Apollo 10 named their spacecraft *Charlie Brown* and *Snoopy*,
assistant manager for public affairs [Julian Scheer](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") wrote to [George Low](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), the Manager of the Apollo Spacecraft Program Office at the MSC, to suggest the Apollo 11 crew be less flippant in naming their craft. The name
*Snowcone* was used for the CM and *Haystack* was used for the LM in both internal
and external communications during early mission planning.[[73]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

The LM was named *[Eagle](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")*
after the motif which was featured prominently on the mission insignia. At Scheer's
suggestion, the CM was named *[Columbia](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")*
after *[Columbiad](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")*, the giant cannon that launched a spacecraft (also
from Florida) in [Jules Verne](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")'s 1865 novel *[From the Earth to the Moon](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")*. It also referred to [Columbia](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), a historical name of the United
States.[[74]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[75]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
In Collins' 1976 book, he said *Columbia* was in reference to [Christopher Columbus](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").[[76]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")


### Mementos
[![application/atom+xml](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:CentralAutoLogin/start?useformat=desktop&type=script&usesul3=1 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Apollo 11 space-flown silver [Robbins medallion](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The astronauts had [personal preference kits](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (PPKs), small bags containing personal items of significance they wanted to take with them on the
mission.[[77]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Five 0.5-pound (0.23 kg) PPKs were carried on Apollo 11: three (one for each
astronaut) were stowed on *Columbia* before launch, and two on *Eagle*.[[78]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

Neil Armstrong's LM PPK contained a piece of wood from the [Wright brothers](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")' 1903 *[Wright Flyer](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")*'s left propeller and a piece of fabric from its
wing,[[79]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
along with a diamond-studded [astronaut pin](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") originally given to Slayton by the widows of the
Apollo 1 crew. This pin had been intended to be flown on that mission and given
to Slayton afterwards, but following the disastrous launch pad fire and subsequent
funerals, the widows gave the pin to Slayton. Armstrong took it with him on Apollo
11.[[80]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
