[![application/atom+xml](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:CentralAutoLogin/start?useformat=desktop&type=script&usesul3=1 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")


[![application/atom+xml](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:CentralAutoLogin/start?useformat=desktop&type=script&usesul3=1 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")


[![application/atom+xml](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:CentralAutoLogin/start?useformat=desktop&type=script&usesul3=1 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")


[![application/atom+xml](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:CentralAutoLogin/start?useformat=desktop&type=script&usesul3=1 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")


[![application/atom+xml](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:CentralAutoLogin/start?useformat=desktop&type=script&usesul3=1 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

A map of the Moon showing prospective landing sites for Apollo 11. Site 2 in the
[Sea of Tranquility](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") was chosen.

NASA's Apollo Site Selection Board announced five potential landing sites on February
8, 1968. These were the result of two years' worth of studies based on high-resolution
photography of the lunar surface by the five uncrewed probes of the [Lunar Orbiter program](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") and information about surface conditions provided by the [Surveyor program](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").[[81]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The best Earth-bound telescopes could not resolve features with the resolution Project
Apollo required.[[82]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The landing site had to be close to the lunar equator to minimize the amount of propellant
required, clear of obstacles to minimize maneuvering, and flat to simplify the task
of the landing radar. Scientific value was not a consideration.[[83]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

Areas that appeared promising on photographs taken on Earth were often found to be
totally unacceptable. The original requirement that the site be free of craters had
to be relaxed, as no such site was found.[[84]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Five sites were considered: Sites 1 and 2 were in the Sea of Tranquility
(*[Mare Tranquillitatis](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")*); Site 3 was in the Central Bay (*[Sinus Medii](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")*); and Sites 4 and 5 were in the Ocean
of Storms (*[Oceanus Procellarum](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")*).[[81]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")The final site selection was based on seven criteria:

- The site needed to be smooth, with relatively few craters;
- with approach paths free of large hills, tall cliffs or deep craters that might confuse the landing radar and cause it to issue incorrect readings;
- reachable with a minimum amount of propellant;
- allowing for delays in the launch countdown;
- providing the Apollo spacecraft with a free-return trajectory, one that would allow it to coast around the Moon and safely return to Earth without requiring any engine firings should a problem arise on the way to the Moon;
- with good visibility during the landing approach, meaning the Sun would be between 7 and 20 degrees behind the LM; and
- a general slope of less than two degrees in the landing area.[[81]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

The requirement for the Sun angle was particularly restrictive, limiting the launch
date to one day per month.[[81]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
A landing just after dawn was chosen to limit the temperature extremes the astronauts
would experience.[[85]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The Apollo Site Selection Board selected Site 2, with Sites 3 and 5
as backups in the event of the launch being delayed. In May 1969, Apollo 10's lunar
module flew to within 15 kilometers (9.3 mi) of Site 2, and reported it
was acceptable.[[86]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[87]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")


### First-step decision

During the first press conference after the Apollo 11 crew was announced, the first
question was, "Which one of you gentlemen will be the first man to step onto the
lunar surface?"[[88]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[89]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Slayton told the reporter it had not been decided, and Armstrong added that it was
"not based on individual desire".[[88]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

One of the first versions of the egress checklist had the lunar module pilot exit
the spacecraft before the commander, which matched what had been done on Gemini missions,[[90]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
where the commander had never performed the spacewalk.[[91]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Reporters wrote in early 1969 that Aldrin would be the first man to walk on the Moon,
and Associate Administrator [George Mueller](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") told reporters he would be first as well. Aldrin heard that Armstrong would be the first because Armstrong was a civilian, which made Aldrin livid. Aldrin attempted to persuade other Lunar Module pilots he should be first, but they responded cynically about what they perceived as a lobbying campaign. Attempting to stem interdepartmental conflict, Slayton told Aldrin that Armstrong would be first since he was the commander. The decision was announced in a press conference on April 14,
1969.[[92]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

For decades, Aldrin believed the final decision was largely driven by the Lunar Module's
hatch location. Because the astronauts had their spacesuits on and the spacecraft
was so small, maneuvering to exit the spacecraft was difficult. The crew tried a
simulation in which Aldrin left the spacecraft first, but he damaged the simulator
while attempting to egress. While this was enough for mission planners to make their
decision, Aldrin and Armstrong were left in the dark on the decision until late spring.[[93]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Slayton told Armstrong the plan was to have him leave the spacecraft first, if he
agreed. Armstrong said, "Yes, that's the way to do it."[[94]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

The media accused Armstrong of exercising his commander's prerogative to exit the
spacecraft first.[[95]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
[Chris Kraft](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") revealed in his 2001 autobiography that a meeting occurred between Gilruth, Slayton, Low, and himself to make sure Aldrin would not be the first to walk on the Moon. They argued that the first person to walk on the Moon should be like [Charles Lindbergh](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia"), a calm and quiet person. They made the decision to change the flight plan so the commander was the first to egress from the
spacecraft.[[96]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")


### Pre-launch
[![application/atom+xml](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:CentralAutoLogin/start?useformat=desktop&type=script&usesul3=1 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
Saturn V SA-506, the rocket carrying the Apollo 11 spacecraft, moves out of the [Vehicle Assembly Building](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") towards [Launch Complex 39](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia").
The ascent stage of [LM-5 *Eagle*](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") arrived at the [Kennedy Space Center](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") on January 8, 1969, followed by the descent stage four days later, and [CSM-107
*Columbia*](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") on January
23.[[6]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
There were several differences between *Eagle* and Apollo 10's LM-4 *Snoopy*; *Eagle*
had a VHF radio antenna to facilitate communication with the astronauts during their
EVA on the lunar surface; a lighter ascent engine; more thermal protection on the
landing gear; and a package of scientific experiments known as the [Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") (EASEP). The only change in the configuration of the command module was the removal of some insulation from the forward
hatch.[[97]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 -
Wikipedia")[[98]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
The CSM was mated on January 29, and moved from the [Operations and Checkout Building](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") to the [Vehicle Assembly Building](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") on April
14.[[6]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")

The [S-IVB](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") third stage of Saturn V AS-506 had arrived on January 18, followed by the [S-II](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") second stage on February 6, [S-IC](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") first stage on February 20, and the [Saturn V Instrument Unit](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") on February 27. At 12:30 on May 20, the
5,443-tonne (5,357-long-ton; 6,000-short-ton) assembly departed the Vehicle Assembly
Building atop the [crawler-transporter](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia"), bound for Launch Pad 39A, part of [Launch Complex 39](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia"), while Apollo 10 was still on its way to the Moon. A countdown test commenced on June 26, and concluded on July 2. The launch complex was floodlit on the night of July 15, when the crawler-transporter carried the [mobile service structure](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") back to its parking
area.[[6]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
In the early hours of the morning, the fuel tanks of the S-II and S-IVB stages were
filled with [liquid hydrogen](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 -
Wikipedia").[[99]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
Fueling was completed by three hours before launch.[[100]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
Launch operations were partly automated, with 43 programs written in the [ATOLL programming language](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 -
Wikipedia").[[101]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "client-js vector-feature-language-in-header-enabled vector-feature-language-in-main-menu-disabled vector-feature-language-in-main-page-header-disabled vector-feature-page-tools-pinned-disabled vector-feature-toc-pinned-clientpref-1 vector-feature-main-menu-pinned-disabled vector-feature-limited-width-clientpref-1 vector-feature-limited-width-content-enabled vector-feature-custom-font-size-clientpref-1 vector-feature-appearance-pinned-clientpref-1 skin-theme-clientpref-day vector-sticky-header-enabled vector-toc-available skin-thumbsize-clientpref-standard")

Slayton roused the crew shortly after 04:00, and they showered, shaved, and had the
traditional pre-flight breakfast of steak and eggs with Slayton and the backup crew.
They then donned their space suits and began breathing pure oxygen. At 06:30, they
headed out to Launch Complex 39.[[102]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles")
Haise entered *Columbia* about three hours and ten minutes before launch time. Along
with a technician, he helped Armstrong into the left-hand couch at 06:54. Five minutes
later, Collins joined him, taking up his position on the right-hand couch. Finally,
Aldrin entered, taking the center couch.[[100]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Haise left around two hours and ten minutes before launch.[[103]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The closeout crew sealed the hatch, and the cabin was purged and pressurized. The
closeout crew then left the launch complex about an hour before launch time. The
countdown became automated at three minutes and twenty seconds before launch time.[[100]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Over 450 personnel were at the consoles in the [firing room](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").[[99]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")


## Mission


### Launch and flight to lunar orbit
[![application/atom+xml](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=startup&only=scripts&raw=1&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The Apollo 11 Saturn V space vehicle lifts off with astronauts Neil A. Armstrong,
Michael Collins and Edwin E. Aldrin Jr. at 9:32 am. EDT July 16, 1969, from
Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39A.
An estimated one million spectators watched the launch of Apollo 11 from the highways
and beaches in the vicinity of the launch site. Dignitaries included the [Chief of Staff of the United States Army](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), [General](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") [William Westmoreland](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), four [cabinet members](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), 19 [state governors](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), 40 [mayors](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), 60 ambassadors and 200 [congressmen](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"). Vice President [Spiro Agnew](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") viewed the launch with former president [Lyndon B. Johnson](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") and his wife [Lady Bird Johnson](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").[[99]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[104]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Around 3,500 media representatives were present.[[105]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
About two-thirds were from the United States; the rest came from 55 other countries.
The launch was televised live in 33 countries, with an estimated 25 million
viewers in the United States alone. Millions more around the world listened to radio
broadcasts.[[104]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[99]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
President [Richard Nixon](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") viewed the launch from his office in the [White House](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") with his NASA liaison officer, Apollo astronaut [Frank Borman](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").[[106]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Lodging near Cape Canaveral was reported as being booked months ahead in advance
for the launch by a Florida newspaper.[[107]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

Saturn V AS-506 launched Apollo 11 on July 16, 1969, at 13:32:00 [UTC](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (9:32:00 [EDT](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")).[[6]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
At 13.2 seconds into the flight, the vehicle began to [roll](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") into its [flight azimuth](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") of 72.058°. Full shutdown of the first-stage engines occurred about
2 minutes and 42 seconds into the mission, followed by separation of the S-IC
and ignition of the S-II engines. The second stage engines then cut off and separated
at about 9 minutes and 8 seconds, allowing the first ignition of the S-IVB
engine a few seconds later.[[8]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

Apollo 11 entered a [near-circular Earth orbit](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") at an altitude of
100.4 nautical miles (185.9 km) by 98.9 nautical miles (183.2 km), twelve
minutes into its flight. After one and a half orbits, which took around two and a
half hours, a second ignition of the S-IVB engine pushed the spacecraft onto its
trajectory toward the Moon with the [trans-lunar injection](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (TLI) burn, which took about 5 minutes and 47 seconds and started at 16:16:16 UTC. About 30 minutes later, with Collins in the left seat and at the controls, the [transposition, docking, and extraction](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") maneuver was performed. This involved separating
*Columbia* from the spent S-IVB stage, turning around, and docking with *Eagle*
still attached to the stage. After the LM was extracted, the combined spacecraft
headed for the Moon, while the rocket stage flew on a trajectory past the Moon.[[108]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[8]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
This was done to avoid the third stage colliding with the spacecraft, the Earth,
or the Moon. A [slingshot effect](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") from passing around the Moon threw it into an [orbit around the Sun](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").[[109]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

On July 19 at 17:21:50 UTC, Apollo 11 passed behind the Moon and fired its service
propulsion engine to enter [lunar orbit](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").[[8]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[110]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
In the thirty orbits that followed, the crew saw passing views of their landing site
in the southern Sea of Tranquility about 12 miles (19 km) southwest of the crater
[Sabine D](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"). The site was selected in part because it had been characterized as relatively flat and smooth by the automated [Ranger 8](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") and [Surveyor 5](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") landers and the Lunar Orbiter mapping spacecraft, and because it was unlikely to present major landing or EVA
challenges.[[111]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
It lay about 25 kilometers (16 mi) southeast of the Surveyor 5 landing
site, and 68 kilometers (42 mi) southwest of Ranger 8's crash site.[[112]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")


### Lunar descent
[![application/atom+xml](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:CentralAutoLogin/start?useformat=desktop&type=script&usesul3=1 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
[*Columbia*](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") in lunar orbit, photographed from
[*Eagle*](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
At 12:52:00 UTC on July 20, Aldrin and Armstrong entered [*Eagle*](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), and began the final preparations for lunar
descent.[[8]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
At 17:44:00 *Eagle* separated from *Columbia*.[[13]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Collins, alone aboard *Columbia*, inspected *Eagle* as it pirouetted before him to
ensure the craft was not damaged, and that the landing gear was correctly deployed.[[113]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[114]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Armstrong exclaimed: "The *Eagle* has wings!"[[114]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

As the descent began, Armstrong and Aldrin found themselves passing landmarks on
the surface two or three seconds early, and reported that they were "long"; they
would land miles west of their target point. *Eagle* was traveling too fast. The
problem could have been [mascons](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")—concen­tra­tions of high mass in a region or
regions of the Moon's crust that contains a [gravitational anomaly](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), potentially altering
*Eagle*'s trajectory. Flight Director Gene Kranz speculated that it could have resulted
from extra air pressure in the docking tunnel, or a result of *Eagle*'s pirouette
maneuver.[[115]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[116]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

Five minutes into the descent burn, and 6,000 feet (1,800 m) above the surface
of the Moon, the [LM guidance computer](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (LGC) distracted the crew with the first of several unexpected 1201 and 1202 program alarms. Inside Mission Control Center, computer engineer [Jack Garman](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") told [Guidance Officer](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") [Steve Bales](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") it was safe to continue the descent, and this was relayed to the crew. The program alarms indicated "executive overflows", meaning the guidance computer could not complete all its tasks in real-time and had to postpone some of
them.[[117]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[118]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
[Margaret Hamilton](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), the Director of Apollo Flight Computer Programming at the [MIT](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") [Charles Stark Draper Laboratory](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") later recalled:
[![application/atom+xml](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:CentralAutoLogin/start?useformat=desktop&type=script&usesul3=1 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
[*Eagle*](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") in [lunar orbit](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") photographed from
[*Columbia*](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")"}},"i":0}}]}">
> To blame the computer for the Apollo 11 problems is like blaming the person who
spots a fire and calls the fire department. Actually, the computer was programmed
to do more than recognize error conditions. A complete set of recovery programs was
incorporated into the software. The software's action, in this case, was to eliminate
lower priority tasks and re-establish the more important ones. The computer, rather
than almost forcing an abort, prevented an abort. If the computer hadn't recognized
this problem and taken recovery action, I doubt if Apollo 11 would have been the
successful Moon landing it was.[[119]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

During the mission, the cause was diagnosed as the rendezvous radar switch being
in the wrong position, causing the computer to process data from both the rendezvous
and landing radars at the same time.[[120]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[121]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Software engineer [Don Eyles](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") concluded in a 2005 Guidance and Control Conference paper that the problem was due to a hardware design bug previously seen during testing of the first uncrewed LM in [Apollo 5](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"). Having the rendezvous radar on (so it was warmed up in case of an emergency landing abort) should have been irrelevant to the computer, but an electrical phasing mismatch between two parts of the rendezvous radar system could cause the stationary antenna to appear to the computer as dithering back and forth between two positions, depending upon how the hardware randomly powered up. The extra spurious [cycle stealing](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia"), as the rendezvous radar updated an involuntary counter, caused the computer
alarms.[[122]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")


### Landing
Armstrong pilots *Eagle* to its landing on the Moon, July 20, 1969.
When Armstrong again looked outside, he saw that the computer's landing system was
targeting a boulder-strewn area just north and east of a 300-foot-diameter (91 m)
crater (later determined to be [West crater](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")), so he took semi-automatic
control.[[123]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 -
Wikipedia")[[124]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
Armstrong considered landing short of the boulder field so they could collect geological
samples from it, but could not since their horizontal velocity was too high. Throughout
the descent, Aldrin called out navigation data to Armstrong, who was busy piloting
*Eagle*.[[125]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")

Armstrong found a clear patch of ground and maneuvered the spacecraft towards it.
As he got closer, now 250 feet (76 m) above the surface, he discovered his new
landing site had a crater in it.  Now 107 feet (33 m) above the surface, Armstrong
knew their propellant supply was dwindling and was determined to land at the first
possible landing site. He cleared the crater and found another patch of level ground.
They were now 100 feet (30 m) from the surface, with only 90 seconds of propellant
remaining. Lunar dust kicked up by the LM's engine began to impair his ability to
determine the spacecraft's motion. Some large rocks jutted out of the dust cloud,
and Armstrong focused on them during his descent so he could determine the spacecraft's
speed.[[126]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")

A light informed Aldrin that at least one of the 67-inch (170 cm) probes hanging
from *Eagle*'s footpads had touched the surface a few moments before the landing
and he said: "Contact light!" Armstrong was supposed to immediately shut the engine
down, as the engineers suspected the pressure caused by the engine's own exhaust
reflecting off the lunar surface could make it explode, but he forgot. Three seconds
later, *Eagle* landed and Armstrong shut the engine down.[[127]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles")
Aldrin immediately said "Okay, engine stop. ACA—out of [detent](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles")." Armstrong acknowledged: "Out of detent. Auto." Aldrin continued: "Mode control—both auto. Descent engine command override off. Engine arm—off. 413 is
in."[[128]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
[![application/atom+xml](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=startup&only=scripts&raw=1&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The landing site relative to [West crater](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
ACA was the [Attitude Control Assembly](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")—the LM's control stick. Output went to the LGC to command the [reaction control system](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (RCS) jets to fire. "Out of Detent" meant the stick had moved away from its centered position; it was spring-centered like the turn indicator in a car. Address 413 of the [Abort Guidance System](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (AGS) contained the variable that indicated the LM had
landed.[[10]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

*Eagle* landed at 20:17:40 UTC on Sunday July 20 with 216 pounds (98 kg) of
usable fuel remaining. Information available to the crew and mission controllers
during the landing showed the LM had enough fuel for another 25 seconds of powered
flight before an abort without touchdown would have become unsafe,[[10]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[129]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
but post-mission analysis showed that the real figure was probably closer to 50 seconds.[[130]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Apollo 11 landed with less fuel than most subsequent missions, and the astronauts
encountered a premature low fuel warning. This was later found to be the result of
the propellant [sloshing](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") more than expected, uncovering a fuel sensor. On subsequent missions, extra [anti-slosh baffles](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") were added to the tanks to prevent
this.[[10]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

Armstrong acknowledged Aldrin's completion of the post-landing checklist with "Engine
arm is off", before responding to the CAPCOM, Charles Duke, with the words, "Houston,
[Tranquility Base](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") here. The *[Eagle](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")*
has landed." Armstrong's unrehearsed change of call sign from "Eagle" to "Tranquility
Base" emphasized to listeners that landing was complete and successful.[[131]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[*[better source needed](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")*] Duke expressed the relief at Mission Control: "Roger,
Twan—Tranquility, we copy you on the ground. You got a bunch of guys about to turn
blue. We're breathing again. Thanks a lot."[[10]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[132]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
A [3-D](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") view from the [Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (LRO) of the Apollo 11 landing site
Two and a half hours after landing, before preparations began for the EVA, Aldrin
radioed to Earth:
"}},"i":0}}]}">
> This is the LM pilot. I'd like to take this opportunity to ask every person listening
in, whoever and wherever they may be, to pause for a moment and contemplate the events
of the past few hours and to give thanks in his or her own way.[[133]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

He then took [communion](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") privately. At this time NASA was still fighting a lawsuit brought by atheist [Madalyn Murray O'Hair](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (who had objected to the
[Apollo 8 crew reading from the Book of Genesis](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")) demanding that their astronauts refrain from broadcasting religious activities while in space. For this reason, Aldrin chose to refrain from directly mentioning taking communion on the Moon. Aldrin was an elder at the [Webster](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") [Presbyterian Church](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles"), and his communion kit was prepared by the pastor of the church, Dean Woodruff. Webster Presbyterian possesses the chalice used on the Moon and commemorates the event each year on the Sunday closest to July
20.[[134]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The schedule for the mission called for the astronauts to follow the landing with
a five-hour sleep period, but they chose to begin preparations for the EVA early,
thinking they would be unable to sleep.[[135]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")


### Lunar surface operations

Main article: [Tranquility Base](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Preparations for [Neil Armstrong](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") and [Buzz Aldrin](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") to walk on the Moon began at 23:43
UTC.[[13]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
These took longer than expected; three and a half hours instead of two.[[136]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
During training on Earth, everything required had been neatly laid out in advance,
but on the Moon the cabin contained a large number of other items as well, such as
checklists, food packets, and tools.[[137]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Six hours and thirty-nine minutes after landing, Armstrong and Aldrin were ready
to go outside, and *Eagle* was depressurized.[[138]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

*Eagle*'s hatch was opened at 02:39:33.[[13]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Armstrong initially had some difficulties squeezing through the hatch with his [portable life support system](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
(PLSS).[[136]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Some of the highest heart rates recorded from Apollo astronauts occurred during LM
egress and ingress.[[139]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
At 02:51 Armstrong began his descent to the lunar surface. The remote-control unit
on his chest kept him from seeing his feet. Climbing down the nine-rung ladder, Armstrong
pulled a D-ring to deploy the modular equipment stowage assembly (MESA) folded against
*Eagle*'s side and activate the TV camera.[[140]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022
"ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")[[141]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

Apollo 11 used [slow-scan television](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") (TV) incompatible with broadcast TV, so it was displayed on a special monitor and a conventional TV camera viewed this monitor (thus, a broadcast of a broadcast), significantly reducing the quality of the
picture.[[142]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The signal was received at [Goldstone](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") in the United States, but with better fidelity by [Honeysuckle Creek Tracking Station](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") near [Canberra](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") in Australia. Minutes later the feed was switched to the more sensitive [Parkes radio telescope](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") in
Australia.[[143]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Despite some technical and weather difficulties, black and white images of the first
lunar EVA were received and broadcast to at least 600 million people on Earth.[[143]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Copies of this video in broadcast format were saved and are widely available, but
[recordings of the original slow scan source transmission from the lunar surface](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") were likely destroyed during routine magnetic tape re-use at
NASA.[[142]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Video of Neil Armstrong and the first step on the Moon

After describing the surface dust as "very fine-grained" and "almost like a powder",[[141]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
at 02:56:15,[[144]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
six and a half hours after landing, Armstrong stepped off *Eagle*'s landing pad and
declared: "That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind."{{cite
web|url=http://history.nasa.gov/alsj/a11/a11.step.html#1092413|title=One Small
Step|last1=Jones|first1=Eric|website=Apollo 11 Lunar Surface Journal|access-date=September
6, 2019|date=April 8, 2018|archive-date=September 3,
2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190903233224/https://history.nasa.gov/alsj/a11/a11.step.html#1092413|url-status=live}}"},"name":{"wt":"transcript"}},"i":0}}]}">[[b]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 -
Wikipedia")[[146]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 -
Wikipedia")[[147]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")

Armstrong intended to say "That's one small step for a man", but the word "a" is
not audible in the transmission, and thus was not initially reported by most observers
of the live broadcast. When later asked about his quote, Armstrong said he believed
he said "for a man", and subsequent printed versions of the quote included the "a"
in square brackets. One explanation for the absence may be that his accent caused
him to slur the words "for a" together; another is the intermittent nature of the
audio and video links to Earth, partly because of storms near Parkes Observatory.
A more recent digital analysis of the tape claims to reveal the "a" may have been
spoken but obscured by static. Other analysis points to the claims of static and
slurring as "face-saving fabrication", and that Armstrong himself later admitted
to misspeaking the line.[[148]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 -
Wikipedia")[[149]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 -
Wikipedia")[[150]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")

About seven minutes after stepping onto the Moon's surface, Armstrong collected a
contingency soil sample using a sample bag on a stick. He then folded the bag and
tucked it into a pocket on his right thigh. This was to guarantee there would be
some lunar soil brought back in case an emergency required the astronauts to abandon
the EVA and return to the LM.[[151]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
Twelve minutes after the sample was collected,[[146]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
he removed the TV camera from the MESA and made a panoramic sweep, then mounted it
on a tripod.[[136]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
The TV camera cable remained partly coiled and presented a tripping hazard throughout
the EVA. Still photography was accomplished with a [Hasselblad](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia") camera that could be operated hand-held or mounted on Armstrong's [Apollo space suit](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 -
Wikipedia").[[152]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "Apollo 11 - Wikipedia")
Aldrin joined Armstrong on the surface. He described the view with the simple phrase:
"Magnificent desolation."[[141]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "client-js vector-feature-language-in-header-enabled vector-feature-language-in-main-menu-disabled vector-feature-language-in-main-page-header-disabled vector-feature-page-tools-pinned-disabled vector-feature-toc-pinned-clientpref-1 vector-feature-main-menu-pinned-disabled vector-feature-limited-width-clientpref-1 vector-feature-limited-width-content-enabled vector-feature-custom-font-size-clientpref-1 vector-feature-appearance-pinned-clientpref-1 skin-theme-clientpref-day vector-sticky-header-enabled vector-toc-available skin-thumbsize-clientpref-standard")

Armstrong said moving in the [lunar gravity](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "client-js vector-feature-language-in-header-enabled vector-feature-language-in-main-menu-disabled vector-feature-language-in-main-page-header-disabled vector-feature-page-tools-pinned-disabled vector-feature-toc-pinned-clientpref-1 vector-feature-main-menu-pinned-disabled vector-feature-limited-width-clientpref-1 vector-feature-limited-width-content-enabled vector-feature-custom-font-size-clientpref-1 vector-feature-appearance-pinned-clientpref-1 skin-theme-clientpref-day vector-sticky-header-enabled vector-toc-available skin-thumbsize-clientpref-standard"), one-sixth of Earth's, was "even perhaps easier than the
simulations ... It's absolutely no trouble to walk around."[[141]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ext.globalCssJs.user.styles")
Aldrin joined him on the surface and tested methods for moving around, including
two-footed kangaroo hops. The PLSS backpack created a tendency to tip backward, but
neither astronaut had serious problems maintaining balance. Loping became the preferred
method of movement. The astronauts reported that they needed to plan their movements
six or seven steps ahead. The fine soil was quite slippery. Aldrin remarked that
moving from sunlight into *Eagle*'s shadow produced no temperature change inside
the suit, but the helmet was warmer in sunlight, so he felt cooler in shadow.[[141]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
The MESA failed to provide a stable work platform and was in shadow, slowing work
somewhat. As they worked, the moonwalkers kicked up gray dust, which soiled the outer
part of their suits.[[152]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
[![application/atom+xml](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=startup&only=scripts&raw=1&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Aldrin salutes the deployed United States flag on the [lunar surface](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles").
The astronauts planted the [Lunar Flag Assembly](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") containing a [flag of the United States](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles") on the lunar surface, in clear view of the TV camera. Aldrin remembered, "Of all the jobs I had to do on the Moon the one I wanted to go the smoothest was the flag
raising."[[153]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
But the astronauts struggled with the telescoping rod and could only insert the pole
about 2 inches (5 cm) into the hard lunar surface. Aldrin was afraid it might
topple in front of TV viewers, but gave "a crisp West Point salute".[[153]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")

Before Aldrin could take a photo of Armstrong with the flag, President Richard Nixon
spoke to them through a telephone-radio transmission, which Nixon called "the most
historic phone call ever made from the White House."[[154]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=ext.cite.parsoid.styles%7Cext.cite.styles%7Cext.tmh.player.styles%7Cext.uls.interlanguage%7Cext.visualEditor.desktopArticleTarget.noscript%7Cext.wikimediaBadges%7Cext.wikimediaBadges.ulsV2%7Cext.wikimediamessages.styles%7Cjquery.makeCollapsible.styles%7Cmediawiki.skinning.content.parsoid%7Cmediawiki.skins.legacy%7Cskins.vector.icons%2Cstyles%7Cskins.vector.search.codex.styles%7Cwikibase.client.init&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
Nixon originally had a long speech prepared to read during the phone call, but Frank
Borman, who was at the White House as a NASA liaison during Apollo 11, convinced
Nixon to keep his words brief.[[155]](/w/load.php?lang=en&modules=site.styles&only=styles&skin=vector-2022 "ResourceLoaderDynamicStyles")
